content_html:
Hey folks. We have just crossed Rebound Capital’s 1st Anniversary, and I want to thank every one of you. The fact that nearly 23,000 of you read my content is a big responsibility. I will keep grinding and doing what I love - finding value in the stock market.

Last month, we derisked the portfolio from the AI theme. June gave us a preview of why that was important. More on that later.

Rebound Portfolio Performance

Happy to report that the Rebound portfolio is now beating the market (S&P 500) since inception (in Aug’25) by ~4%.

Our portfolio experienced a significant drawdown in Feb-March, driven by AI doomerism and the Iran War. Drawdowns are always tough. But we stuck to our core principles, and that discipline is why we are outperforming the market by ~13% since it bottomed on March 30th. Taking advantage of the downturn, we invested in mispriced stocks, with 1 investment ~3x for us (starting at ~8% of the portfolio and trimmed last month).

We pulled ahead in a market where a handful of AI names have been carrying the index, and we did it because we don’t buy cheap for its own sake. We pair value with embedded catalysts - a discounted stock only interests us when the market is also materially underestimating where its earnings and key metrics are headed over the next 6 to 24 months. Cheap can stay cheap forever. The re-rating comes when the market is forced to upgrade its consensus estimates for those material KPIs.

What We Are Focused On

Looking ahead, we are focused on three things:

Calibrating our thesis on Semis: The AI cycle is real, and companies are still early in AI implementation. But the stock prices of most AI and semiconductor stocks are, in our estimate, at the later stages of their bull run. Stock selection is key.

In late June, semiconductor stocks had a sharp, multi-day pullback as investors took profits in the most stretched winners. But Micron's earnings have reinvigorated the speculative rally. This is exactly the ‘any hiccup will lead to a sharp fall’ dynamic we flagged last month.

We had cut our portfolio’s exposure to AMD and Nvidia last month. We are keeping our reduced semi weights and are ready to trim further on any sharp bounce. The semiconductor companies’ revenues will keep compounding for many years - but the stock may not, especially since they are now so stretched in terms of valuation.

Calibrating our thesis on Big Tech: We are getting incrementally more bullish on megacap technology companies. These stocks have been laggards for 1-2 years now due to the large increase in capital expenditure for building AI data centers.

Their money has been spent on buying increasingly expensive semiconductor chips - whether it is compute from Nvidia, Broadcom, and AMD, or memory from Micron and SK Hynix. The semicap companies have benefited immensely as well, rising 3x-4x from just 18 months ago. Going ahead, we see the following happening:

  • Big tech will cut costs by designing custom compute (ASICs) and finding more efficient ways to use memory.

  • A pause or a second look at capital expenditure on building out AI data centers may be around the corner. Many executives at these companies are paid in stock, and there is no rationale in letting Micron make 80%+ gross margins at the expense of their own stock prices.

  • Many companies are now trying to optimize their AI spending (read Coinbase’s CEO explaining how they are doing it) - and this will also be a catalyst for hyperscalers to revisit their capex plans. Of course, if their cloud revenue growth accelerates materially due to insatiable demand, they may not worry too much about capex. Either way, investors should do fine. Cloud providers are also well positioned to help customers optimize their operations. They can offer cheaper models for less-intensive tasks and frontier models only for the most difficult tasks (in an automated manner). This will shift more of the value in the AI stack towards cloud providers and away from frontier labs and semis.

Quality companies are overlooked amid the AI mania: Multiple names with years of strong growth ahead are now trading at their lowest multiples in a long time (including S&P Global, Visa, Moody’s, Netflix, etc.). We added to one of them this month (more on that below), and we will keep digging.

Portfolio Statistics

My target for the RC portfolio is to achieve a ~15% CAGR over the long term. I think this is meaningful compounding, doubling my wealth every 5 years.

I am focused on compounding and growing my wealth and treat the S&P500’s return as a benchmark to beat - but I don’t expect my strategy will beat it in all conditions. Especially as the market is driven by momentum and trends in many quarters.

Rebound Capital’s portfolio compounds faster than the index while trading at essentially the same valuation. To gauge it, we take a weighted average of each holding’s metrics. The headline numbers:

  • Revenue growth, next 3 years: ~18%

  • EBIT growth, next 3 years: ~19%

  • EV/EBIT: ~26x

Here is the interesting part. Our portfolio is set to compound EBIT at around 19% per year, ahead of the low-to-mid-teens consensus for the S&P 500, and we pay no premium on the multiple to do so (S&P 500 currently trades at ~26x EV/EBIT).

Divide valuation by growth, and the portfolio screens materially cheaper than the index. In short, the RC portfolio compounds faster than the market while costing roughly the same per unit of growth.

Broader Market Commentary

AI remains the market’s driver

The demand for AI is strong. Micron’s late June print was a clear beat and raise, with revenue stepping up enormously year-over-year - a reminder that the AI infrastructure trade is backed by real spend, not just sentiment. We are not bearish on the buildout - we own semis. But we are concerned about the valuations.

So, our posture is unchanged. We still own the buildout through reasonably valued names and will keep trimming where price runs ahead of fundamentals.

Consumer distress is real, and the 2-tier economy persists

The top decile of earners still drives a record share of spending. Businesses catering to the lower-income customers remain under stress. The three sector implications we flagged last month all stand:

Restaurants: still under stress on a third straight year of weak traffic, price pushback, and GLP-1 headwinds. We have done deep dives on Domino’s and Wingstop. We will be on the lookout for opportunities here and remain very strict about the valuations we pay.

Medical devices: still see elective-procedure deferrals, which created our entry into Cochlear. This is a segment with many high-quality companies we are researching. The GLP-1 related headwinds are affecting this group as well (healthier people lead to lower need for medical devices).

High-end luxury: this is where the setup can quickly turn around now that the war has ended and if the trade war/tariffs are not revived.
